extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and counsel appearing before the PTAB (petitioners and patent owners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing and litigating ex parte appeals and AIA post-grant proceedings (IPR, PGR, CBM) before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, covering petitions, responses, institution, discovery, motions, hearings, and final decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition threshold burden
rubrics_metrics.description: The Petition must carry the threshold burden that the Petitioner will prevail with respect to at least one challenged claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institution standards differ by proceeding: IPR requires a reasonable likelihood that Petitioner would prevail on at least one challenged claim; PGR/CBMR require that it is more likely than not that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable. Petition must therefore be drafted to meet the applicable institution standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition must-haves (content requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Petition must identify the Petitioner, real-parties-in-interest, counsel; include a statement of the precise relief requested; and a full statement of the reasons for the relief requested (detailed explanation of why the claims are invalid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR/PGR/CBMR petitioners must include prior art (patents/printed publications) analysis for 102/103; PGR/CBMR must include analysis of 101 and 112 where applicable. Petitions must set forth any claim constructions needed to interpret the claims. CBMR requires additional analysis showing the patent is a CBM and that petitioner has been charged with infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition formatting and form requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Petition must be in size 14, font Times New Roman, and double spaced (with some exceptions); claim charts can be single spaced; petitions have strict word limits and no incorporation of arguments by reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word limits: IPR petitions — 14,000 words; PGR/CBMR petitions — 18,700 words. No incorporation by reference to other documents for substantive arguments; PTAB may authorize corrected Petitions for minor informalities but you get only one chance to submit a winning Petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard
rubrics_metrics.description: For Petitions filed on or after November 13, 2018, the PTAB uses the federal court claim construction standard (Phillips) rather than BRI; for prior petitions the BRI standard may apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When construing claim terms, PTAB will consider any prior claim construction determinations made in a civil action or ITC proceeding if timely made of record. The same Phillips standard applies to proposed substitute claims in motions to amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution standards (IPR vs PGR/CBMR)
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR institution standard: reasonable likelihood that petitioner would prevail on at least one challenged claim. PGR/CBMR institution standard: more likely than not that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These institution standards determine the burden the petitioner must meet at the Petition phase; institution decisions are accompanied by a Scheduling Order and start the one-year clock for Final Written Decision (subject to limited extensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible patents and petitioners for IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligible patents: all non-AIA patents; and AIA patents after nine months of grant or after termination of a PGR. Eligible petitioners: any individual or entity who is not the Patent Owner, subject to certain bars (civil action filed by petitioner or one-year time bar, estoppel). Eligible grounds: 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 and 103 based on patents and printed publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner may be barred if it or its real party-in-interest filed a civil action challenging the patent, if petition is filed more than one year after being served with an infringement complaint, or if estopped from challenging on grounds in the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible patents and petitioners for PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligible patents: AIA patents no later than nine months from the date of grant. Eligible petitioners: any individual or entity who is not the Patent Owner, subject to civil-action and estoppel bars. Eligible grounds: all available grounds under 35 U.S.C. §282(b)(2) or (3) (includes 101, 112, 102, 103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR allows challenges broader than IPR (e.g., 101 and 112) but is time-limited to within nine months of grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered Business Method reviews apply to non-AIA and AIA 'financial services' patents (nine months after grant for AIA), excluding 'technological inventions.' Petitioner must have been sued or charged with infringement (or be the proper party) and is subject to the same civil-action and estoppel bars as other proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligible grounds include all available 35 U.S.C. §282(b)(2) or (3) grounds except as modified by AIA §18(a)(1)(C). Familiarity with AIA §18 and Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner faces estoppel on 'any ground that the Petitioner raised or reasonably could have raised' (PTO estoppel) and similar language applies in district courts/ITC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the scope of later estoppel under 35 U.S.C. §§ 315(e), 325(e) when selecting grounds and presenting prior art in the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real party-in-interest (RPI) burden and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The IPR petitioner bears the burden of persuading the Board that the petition is not time-barred under §315(b); the Board should accept the petitioner's initial identification of RPIs unless disputed by patent owner; the patent owner must produce 'some evidence' that a third party should have been named an RPI (Worlds Inc. v. Bungie).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RPI is 'the party that desires review of the patent' and may include parties at whose behest the petition is filed. Determination of RPI is flexible and fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privy (privity) factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Privity is an inquiry into whether parties have a 'substantive legal relationship' (Taylor v. Sturgell). The Trial Practice Guide uses Taylor factors to analyze privity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taylor factors include: (1) agreement that non-party be bound; (2) pre-existing substantive legal relationship; (3) representation in an action by someone with same interests; (4) assumption of control over an action by non-party; (5) relitigation through a proxy; (6) existence of a special statutory scheme. Use these to assess whether a nonparty is a privy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 112 issues in IPR/PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112 issues cannot be raised in an IPR. However, Section 112 can arise in IPR when determining earliest effective filing date for prior art application and in the context of whether PGR applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to SAS, PTAB sometimes refused to institute IPRs on claims indefiniteness under 112; post-SAS the Board cannot selectively institute some claims and refuse others on that basis. Consider 112 implications when establishing effective filing dates and applicable prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting prior art — petitioner's burden
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner has the burden of demonstrating that a reference qualifies as prior art and the burden of persuasion remains with the petitioner to prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence under 35 U.S.C. §316(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating prior art selection, consider scope of later estoppel (35 U.S.C. §§ 315(e), 325(e)) and be prepared to establish prior art status and relevance in the petition and supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication eligibility (Klopfenstein factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors for determining whether information qualifies as a printed publication (In re Klopfenstein): (i) length of time the display was exhibited; (ii) expertise of target audience; (iii) reasonable expectations about copying; (iv) simplicity/ease of copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide contemporaneous evidence in the petition (declarations, indexing evidence, journal release evidence) and consider showing multiple instances of publication. See USPTO Best Practices for Proving a Document is a Printed Publication (Dec. 7, 2017).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies for qualifying printed publications
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on an article or publication, petitioners are required to establish references as printed publications and should provide supporting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of evidence: declarations from persons with personal knowledge regarding the publication, evidence of library indexing, evidence of release in a well-known journal, and showing multiple instances of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Owner Preliminary Response (POPR) timing and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Any POPR is due within three months of a Notice of Filing Date Accorded (not petition filing date). Rules now allow Patent Owners to submit new testimonial evidence with the Preliminary Response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For institution decisions, the Board will find any dispute of material fact in favor of Petitioner. POPR should therefore focus on legal arguments against institution (statutory bars, estoppel, incomplete petition, failure to meet thresholds) and on highlighting weaknesses in prior art or claim elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: POPR substantive arguments to defeat institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Owner may argue statutory bars (e.g., one-year window for IPR, lack of being sued/charged for CBMR, estoppel), that petition is incomplete (e.g., missing claim constructions), or that petition fails to meet institution thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider arguing that prior art lacks a material element of the claims, teaches away, or does not qualify as prior art. Board has discretion to deny institution based on redundancy or prior consideration by the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board's discretion and Director-delegated considerations (§§ 314(a), 324(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board considers various non-exclusive factors in determining whether to institute trial; §§ 314(a) and 324(a) provide the Director with discretion to deny a petition (e.g., to prevent abuse by repeated attacks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General Plastic and related authorities enumerate non-exclusive factors the Board will consider when exercising discretion on institution, particularly for follow-on petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Plastic non-exclusive factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider for discretionary denial (General Plastic): (1) whether same petitioner previously filed a petition on same claims; (2) knowledge of asserted prior art at time of first petition; (3) whether petitioner received POPR or Board decision on first petition; (4) length of time between learning of prior art and filing second petition; (5) explanation for time elapsed between filings; (6) finite resources of the Board; (7) requirement to issue final determination within 1 year of institution (35 U.S.C. §316(a)(11)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are non-exclusive; weigh them when considering follow-on petitions to anticipate discretionary denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. §325(d) considerations (Becton Dickinson factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Director may reject a petition because the same or substantially the same art or arguments were previously presented to the Office. Becton Dickinson factors include: (1) similarities/material differences between asserted art and prior art during examination; (2) cumulative nature of asserted art vs prior art; (3) extent to which asserted art was evaluated during examination; (4) extent of overlap between arguments made during examination and petition; (5) whether petitioner pointed out how Office erred; (6) extent to which additional evidence in petition warrants reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these factors to assess whether a petition is vulnerable to denial under §325(d) due to rehashing examination record arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder rules and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Board has discretion to join multiple petitions under 35 U.S.C. §315(c). A request for joinder must be filed within one month after the institution date of the petition for which joinder is requested (37 C.F.R. §42.122(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board has addressed edge issues such as whether a time-barred petitioner can join its own prior instituted proceeding and raise new issues; monitor precedent and POP reviews for changing joinder practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution Decision mechanics and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Institution Decision sets out which claims are instituted and under what grounds, is accompanied by a Scheduling Order for trial phase, starts the one-year clock to issue a Final Written Decision, and (post-SAS) the Board will institute as to all claims or none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institution Decisions are final and non-appealable (but reconsideration is an option). Understand scheduling order for deadlines and discovery windows that follow institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery types (routine, mandatory, additional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery during PTAB trial is limited to three types: routine, mandatory, and additional discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine discovery includes serving any exhibit cited in a paper/testimony, serving relevant information inconsistent with a party's position concurrently with filing, and cross-examination of declarants. Mandatory initial disclosures may be agreed to (two options) and additional discovery requires Board authorization if parties do not agree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory initial disclosures options
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may agree to mandatory discovery that requires initial disclosures; Option 1 is modeled after FRCP 26(a), Option 2 is more extensive and generally requires the petitioner to identify persons/information relating to obviousness, secondary considerations, and alleged prior nonpublished public disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Option 2 is more burdensome on petitioner and is rarely agreed to; consider strategic implications before agreeing to mandatory disclosure frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional discovery standard and Garmin factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional discovery beyond routine/mandatory discovery requires a showing that it is in the interests of justice (for IPRs) or for good cause (for PGRs/CBMRs). Garmin factors guide whether to grant additional discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Garmin factors include: (1) more than a possibility that something useful will be found; (2) requests should not seek other party's litigation positions or underlying basis; (3) ability to generate equivalent information by other means; (4) easily understandable instructions; (5) requests not overly burdensome to answer. Use these to draft and oppose additional discovery requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and preservation for objections to evidence (motions to exclude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to evidence must be filed within five business days of service of the evidence or ten days after institution of trial (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.64(a), 42.64(b)(1)). Objections may be preserved only by filing a motion to exclude (37 C.F.R. §42.64(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scheduling order typically sets due dates for motions to exclude, oppositions, and replies. Timely preservation is required to have evidentiary issues considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to strike and authorization practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A party believing the opposing brief raises new issues, belated evidence, or exceeds scope may request authorization to file a motion to strike; alternatively request authorization for further merits briefing such as sur-reply. Authorization to file motion to strike should generally be requested within one week of the allegedly improper submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appropriate, a motion to strike should be tied to the need to address improperly raised matters rather than routine disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to amend claims timing and standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion to Amend Claims is currently due with the Patent Owner Response. A single Motion to Amend may be filed as of right; additional motions require a showing of 'good cause.' The Phillips claim construction standard will be used for proposed substitute claims in a motion to amend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB designated Lectrosonics as precedential regarding motion to amend practice; shape amendment strategy around one motion as of right and the evidentiary record needed to support substituting claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition and reply practice for motions to amend
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner may oppose a motion to amend arguing the amendments do not distinguish over known prior art and may submit new evidence (which triggers new Patent Owner Discovery). Patent Owner Reply in support of motion to amend may submit new evidence (triggering new Petitioner discovery); scope is limited to responding to opposition. Petitioner sur-replies are normally authorized per scheduling order and are scope-limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and manage discovery implications when parties introduce new evidence at amendment stage and use sur-reply practice to maintain scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral hearing requests and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may request oral argument; live testimony may be permitted when requested and approved; demonstrative exhibits may be filed but must include only material from the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board ordinarily provides an hour of argument per side for a single proceeding, but parties may request more or less time; Board encourages conferral and joint agreement on time. Pre-hearing conference calls may preview issues but not argue them; Board may permit brief sur-rebuttal if requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Written Decision timing and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Final Written Decision is required within one year of institution (subject to extension for good cause and joinder); it decides all instituted grounds and if claims are deemed unpatentable the Board will order them 'cancelled'. Issuing the FWD creates estoppel for issues raised (or reasonably could have been raised for IPRs and PGRs) during the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the estoppel consequences and available post-FWD remedies such as rehearing and appeal when counseling clients on settlement and post-trial strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Final Written Decision options (rehearing and appeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rehearing: Any party dissatisfied with the FWD may file one Request for Reconsideration, due 30 days from the FWD. Appeal: Parties may appeal the FWD to the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit; Notice of Appeal due within 63 days unless tolled by a timely rehearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider timing for rehearing vs direct appeal; rehearing tolls appeal filing deadline if timely filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand procedures (SOP 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard Operating Procedure 9 governs cases remanded from the Federal Circuit. The Board aims to issue decisions within 6 months after the Federal Circuit's mandate and provides default procedures on further briefing, evidence, oral hearings, and whether prosecution will be reopened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On remand, expect expedited Board procedures but review SOP9 and Appendix 2 for default handling of evidence and hearings; plan for potential additional proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practices — Appeal Briefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective Appeal Briefs: present only the strongest arguments; strategically group claims to highlight strongest arguments; develop facts to show how law applies; understand burden of proof; define key claim terms; support arguments with evidence; understand difference between appealable and petitionable issues; use Summary of Claimed Subject Matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with judges' expectations: focus, organization, and evidentiary support increase chances of success in ex parte appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practices — Reply Briefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective Reply Briefs: use to respond to points raised in Examiner's Answer; do not reiterate arguments presented in Appeal Brief; do not raise new arguments not responsive to Examiner's Answer; do not separately argue claims for the first time in a Reply Brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep reply focused and strictly responsive to avoid waiver and preserve appropriate scope for appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practices — Rehearing requests
rubrics_metrics.description: File Requests for Rehearing only when appropriate; do not simply re-argue points raised in the briefs; identify particular points of error by the Board; strategically limit arguments to only one or two assertions of error and refer to specific portions of the Board's opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A focused rehearing request that points to discrete legal or factual errors is more likely to be considered than a broad rehash of prior arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practices — Petition drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Dos and don'ts for petitions include number and presentation of grounds, use and content of expert declaration, consider impact of claim construction change, and other strategic matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roundtable suggestions emphasize strategic drafting to meet institution thresholds, careful selection and presentation of prior art, and well-supported expert declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practices — POPR, Institution, Discovery, Trial Briefing, Amendment, Hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: The slides highlight tailored best practices for Patent Owner Preliminary Responses, addressing General Plastic and Becton Dickinson factors at institution, effective motions for discovery, effective trial brief writing, effective amendment briefing, and preparing demonstratives and live testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each stage has specialized tactical considerations: e.g., POPR should focus on statutory bars and thresholds; institution practice should address follow-on petition factors; discovery motions should satisfy Garmin factors; amendment practice should anticipate Lectrosonics precedent; hearing preparation should ensure demonstratives are record-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine discovery obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: A party must serve any exhibit cited in a paper or testimony (unless already served or parties agree otherwise); must serve relevant information inconsistent with a party's position concurrent with the filing of the documents that include the inconsistency; and may cross-examine the other party's declarants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure timely exchange of exhibits and inconsistent information to avoid disputes and to comply with scheduling orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and scope limits for replies, sur-replies, and new evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Replies and sur-replies are generally limited in scope to responding to the immediately prior filing; parties may submit new evidence in replies or opposition but doing so often triggers additional discovery periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be strategic when introducing new evidence because it expands discovery obligations and may prolong the proceeding; coordinate with scheduling order and anticipate procedural consequences.
